We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The "Continue Shopping" button is positioned above "Place Order" in the layout, placing a secondary action higher than the primary checkout action.

B) The "Place Order" label is visually buried below "Continue Shopping", making it harder to locate as the main purpose of the screen.

C) The two buttons are grouped together at the bottom without any section label or separator to distinguish the primary action from the secondary one.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.

turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' drew my eye. Read as the primary action — black fill, more visual prominence than 'Place Order.' The affordance was inverted. Primary-styled button on the secondary action.

turns.q: In a redesigned version of this layout, where would "Place Order" need to appear — and what visual treatment would make it immediately readable as the primary label without scanning the rest of the screen?
turns.a: 'Place Order': solid fill, brand color, white label — standard primary button treatment. 'Continue Shopping': ghost outline or text link — standard secondary treatment. Contrast between the two carries the hierarchy signal. Right now both compete at similar fill weight with the wrong one winning. One CSS pass, two buttons, done.
